tts: Every day, people around the world drink about two point two billion servings of Coca-Cola. It's sold in more than two hundred countries and territories, and for millions of people, its red trucks are the moment the holidays begin. But it started as a medicine, sold by a struggling pharmacist who never got rich from it. It survived a fake bottle war, a world war, and one of the biggest marketing disasters in history. And somewhere along the way, it became tied to Christmas and New Year so tightly that many people think Coke invented Santa Claus. It didn't. So how did a pharmacy syrup become the taste of the holidays? Let's open this bottle.

Our story begins in Atlanta, Georgia, with John Pemberton, a pharmacist and a Confederate veteran who had been wounded at the end of the Civil War. Like many wounded soldiers of his time, he reportedly struggled with morphine, and he spent years mixing tonics and remedies. One of them was a coca wine, copied from a popular French drink. But in eighteen eighty-six, Atlanta voted to ban alcohol. So Pemberton reworked his recipe into a sweet syrup without wine, made with extract from coca leaves and caffeine from kola nuts. His bookkeeper, Frank Robinson, suggested the name, Coca-Cola, and wrote it out in the flowing script that's still on every can today. The syrup was mixed with carbonated water at a pharmacy soda fountain and sold for five cents a glass. In the first year, it sold about nine glasses a day.

Pemberton was sick and short of money, and he sold off pieces of his business before he died in eighteen eighty-eight. The man who ended up with it was Asa Candler, an Atlanta businessman with a genius for marketing. Candler handed out coupons for free glasses, so people would try it once. He put the logo on calendars, clocks, trays and signs, everywhere people looked. The company kept growing, and around the start of the twentieth century, the cocaine was removed from the recipe. In nineteen nineteen, Candler's family sold the company to a group of investors led by Ernest Woodruff for twenty-five million dollars, a huge sum at the time.

Now here's one of the strangest deals in business history. Candler cared about soda fountains, not bottles. So in eighteen ninety-nine, when two lawyers from Chattanooga, Tennessee, asked for the right to bottle the drink, he gave it to them for one dollar. Reportedly, he never even collected the dollar. Those lawyers built a network of local bottling companies, and that idea, a company that makes the syrup and independent partners who bottle and deliver it, is still how the Coca-Cola system works today. It's why a bottle of Coke is made close to where it's sold, almost everywhere on Earth.

But success brought copycats, with names like Koka-Nola and Ko-Kola, in similar straight bottles with similar labels. So in nineteen fifteen, the company asked glassmakers for a bottle so distinctive that you could recognize it by touch in the dark, or even lying broken on the ground. The Root Glass Company in Indiana won. Legend says its designers looked up cocoa in an encyclopedia by mistake and borrowed the shape of the cocoa pod, with its curves and ridges. The contour bottle was patented, and decades later, it became one of the very few packages ever registered as a trademark in the United States. You can probably picture it right now.

Then came the Second World War. Ernest Woodruff's son, Robert, who now ran the company, made a bold promise: every American soldier would get a bottle of Coke for five cents, wherever he was, whatever it cost the company. To keep that promise, bottling plants were built near the front lines, often shipped in pieces and run by technical staff in uniform. When the war ended, those plants stayed, and Coke had a head start in dozens of countries. And in Germany, cut off from the syrup during the war, the local branch invented a new drink from whatever ingredients it could find. They called it Fanta.

After the war, Coke's biggest rival grew stronger. Pepsi had also started in a pharmacy, in eighteen ninety-three, in North Carolina, created by a pharmacist named Caleb Bradham. For decades, the two brands fought what newspapers called the cola wars: cheaper bottles, bigger bottles, celebrity ads, and huge sponsorship deals. The rivalry even went into space. In nineteen eighty-five, astronauts on the space shuttle Challenger tested special cans of both Coke and Pepsi. The verdict was not great: without gravity, the bubbles and the liquid don't separate, and the drinks came out warm and foamy. But here on Earth, the cola wars were about to produce Coca-Cola's most famous mistake.

Fast forward to the nineteen-eighties. Pepsi was running the Pepsi Challenge, blind taste tests where many people picked the sweeter Pepsi. Coca-Cola panicked. After tasting tests with about two hundred thousand people, it changed its century-old formula. In April nineteen eighty-five, New Coke was launched. The reaction was furious. People hoarded cases of the old drink, protest groups formed, and the company's hotline received thousands of angry calls. Just seventy-nine days later, the original came back as Coca-Cola Classic, and it was front-page news across America. Some people still believe it was all a clever trick. The company has always said it was simply a mistake. Either way, people realized they loved the old Coke more than they knew.

Now, Christmas. Coke had a problem: people saw it as a summer drink. So the company started advertising in winter, and in nineteen thirty-one, it hired illustrator Haddon Sundblom to paint Santa Claus. For more than thirty years, Sundblom painted a warm, chubby, rosy-cheeked Santa in a red suit, often taking a break with a Coke. At first, his model was a friend, a retired salesman. Later, Sundblom used his own face in the mirror. Here's the myth: Coke did not invent the red Santa. Cartoonist Thomas Nast drew Santa in red in the eighteen hundreds, and red Santas appeared on magazine covers before nineteen thirty-one. What Coke did was put one consistent, friendly Santa in front of millions of people every December, year after year, until that became the Santa everyone pictures. Later came another winter star: polar bears, which first appeared in a French print ad in nineteen twenty-two, and starred in a famous animated commercial in nineteen ninety-three.

And then the trucks. In nineteen ninety-five, an ad agency created a commercial with a convoy of red trucks covered in lights, rolling through a snowy night, with the jingle Holidays Are Coming. According to the company, each truck in the original ad was decorated with more than thirty thousand bulbs. The ad was shown in more than a hundred countries, and in many places, its first airing each year became an unofficial start of the holiday season. In some countries, real trucks now go on tour, and crowds line up just to take a picture. In Russia, the song was translated as Prazdnik k nam prikhodit, and for a generation, it simply meant: New Year is near.

Today, the company makes far more than one drink, from water to juice to coffee, and its yearly revenue is close to fifty billion dollars. The secret formula is said to be kept in a vault in Atlanta, which visitors can see in the company's museum, though, of course, they can't open it. Legend says only a couple of people know the full recipe at any time. Whether that's true or just great marketing, it's the perfect ending for this story. Because Coca-Cola was never just about what's inside the bottle. It was about a name in a flowing script, a bottle you could recognize in the dark, and a red Santa who showed up every December. And it all started with nine glasses a day in an Atlanta pharmacy.
